utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And good morning to you and Your Honours. Two quick matters, Mr. President. The first concerns a matter agreed upon between the Prosecution and the Defence that relates to the Defence motion -- 67th motion regarding disclosure received by the Prosecution yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I wanted to be sure that microphone is working. Is everybody following Mr. Tieger's submission? Yes. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. We immediately took a look at the motion and attempted to assess the time and word limit required in light of previous motions dealing with the same matter but with fewer witnesses. Our assessment is that we would require 30 days from the date of receipt, that is, yesterday, and an additional 17.000 words, given the number of witnesses implicated. As I mentioned, I discussed this matter with Mr. Robinson and the Defence agrees that this is appropriate and we would ask the Court to grant our request accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, that's granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And the second matter is the Court kindly granted an extension of time on the 22nd of December to address discrepancies between the Registry's assessment of the time consumed and our own internal calculations. That was extremely useful. We have met with the Registry. Those discrepancies have been resolved. I imagine the Court doesn't need any further information on that, but I -- so I wanted to alert the Court accordingly and indicate that the matter had been resolved. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for that information, Mr. Tieger. Yes. Very well. Mr. Karadzic, are you ready to start your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kingori. First of all, are you receiving the translation?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm receiving it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all I would like to thank you for meeting with the Defence. I believe that that will be helpful. At the beginning I would like to ask you, did the military observers of the United Nations have a formulated assignment in writing and did they have any instructions for their work?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are we able to get that paper?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're able to get it, Your Honour, I think through the UN system. But even in my possession I have a piece of paper that entailed our mandate in former Sector East that I worked initially. But for the Srebrenica, I did not take it with myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you trying to say that the assignment and the extent of the work of the observers differed from one locality to the next?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the general work of a military observer is the same everywhere, but there were guide-lines on what to observe in different areas because different areas had different things to look at. There were different issues that were to be observed. Like, if I can give an example, Sector East, where I was initially, there were no open hostilities, especially involving heavy artillery, unlike Srebrenica where there was heavy artillery, heavy machine-gun fire, all the time. So they differed from place to place. There's some areas which were considered to be slightly softer than others. So the issues to look at in those areas differed a bit from the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But this common invariable standard for all military observers was based, first of all, on monitoring and reporting about violations of the cease-fire agreement. Would you agree, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you to look at item B. I think that in the English this is somewhere on the third page, UNMO duties. [In English] General observer duties. [Interpretation] I wanted to ask you something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have only in hard copy?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency. I converted this to Word so that I could make electronic notes because we don't have the full Adobe Acrobat. We only have the Acrobat Reader, so then it's easier for me to convert this file into Word. This is another one of the difficulties. If the demands of the proceedings are so tough in technological terms as well as the pace and we don't have the resources --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I understood. I want to tell you to slow down when you read it. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, I would like to ask you to look at item D -- item B. A is background, B is UNMO duties. What I wanted to ask you was this, I'm a little bit confused because some things in the Sarajevo area that I was close to seem different to me. Are you aware that in the Sarajevo area observers could not cross the line of separation, but rather, some were on the Serbian and some were on the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'm aware is that in the Sarajevo area there was a bit of difference and not just Sarajevo. Even Sector East we had observers on both sides, but Srebrenica we had observers from just inside the enclave. So issues could differ from place to place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You state here in the first sentence, reporting violations to the cease-fire agreement, and then you go on to refer to some activities that I was not aware of about other areas, such as bringing the parties to the table, conducting meetings. Do you know this or do you need to have your amalgamated statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you tasked and was this noted down with bringing the sides together, sitting down with them, and even negotiating about permission to enter or exit the enclave? Are you able to explain this, please, to us?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the aim of us sitting together with both sides of the divide was to make sure that we bring their differences to a close, we reduce their differences. We make sure that we understand why this side is differing from this other side, why they would like to continue with atrocities they were committing in different areas, and then bring them together so that at least there could be peace in the enclave. The aim -- a second aim was to make sure that -- and this is also given -- if you look at my notes, you see somewhere I think is in the statement where Colonel Vukovic was intending to meet Naser Oric and he sent us to tell him that he would like to meet him at a place of his choice, meaning it had reached -- it was now going towards a situation whereby the two antagonists could come together and discuss issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that this was something that you wanted to do from the humanitarian perspective, but did you receive a task in any UN document to mediate between the parties to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, any UN mission in such an area involves a lot of mediation. Mediation was very important and it was there in writing, you mediate between the two warring factions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say "the UN mission," I can understand that. But what did the military observers do specifically? Did you have your own line of command and reporting that was different from the one for UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we had. Our line of reporting was very different from the UNPROFOR one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you read instructions along that same line, instructions and orders?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, UNMOs had their own orders and instructions and a clear mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And was mediation a part of that mandate, mediation and an active relationship with the parties to the conflict, was that something that was part of the MO's duties?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me bring you slightly closer to the issues which were at hand. One, I said at the beginning that UN military observers had a pen and a notebook to record whatever we were discussing and also to make sure that the write-up we make is as strong as possible. The reason for this was whenever you meet one side of the divide, you are to discuss serious issues that they had. Later on you go to this other side, you discuss serious issues that they had. And you are to bring these together. You are to weigh what is making them far apart, stay far apart, and bridge the gap between the two. You can -- you could have done that through the normal chain of command. If it was an issue that was slightly higher than you, you forward the same to the higher levels, so that the mediation could be done at a higher level; or if it was at the operational level, you could do it at your own level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't really want to spend too much time on this question, but it's important for your statement, the amalgamated statement. Other than the human need to help, did you actually receive such an assignment from the United Nations to actively interface with the parties, to mediate between them, or was it your task just to observe and to report back?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were living within -- living and acting within the UN mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And was mediation a part of that mandate as well as what you described?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you followed what I've gone through right now, you'd see mediation was part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when the most observers were present, was the number of you six at the most? I'm talking about the enclave. When there was the greatest number of observers present was that number six?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the highest number we had was six.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm a little confused by the ambitious task placed before the six of you. It says in the same section that: "Another role was to negotiate for permission to leave or even enter the enclave on behalf of other UN agencies and NGOs. Some organisations like the UNHCR, IOM [In English] and all that, could not get access sometimes unless there is an intervention by the UNMOs. Also escort, give escort to some of those organisations so that they are not harmed on the way." [Interpretation] I am wondering that six unarmed people would have such extensive and ambitious assignments, to negotiate about permissions, to protect, to escort. I'm afraid that such a broadly understood assignment had to have led to confusion. Were these tasks that were given to you in keeping with the rules of service for military observers?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, one thing to know is that these were not daily activities. They were not activities being done each and every day. Like asking -- and furthermore it was -- there are things we knew so they were preplanned. Like when there were crossings or food was being brought into the enclave, we would get that report from our headquarters or UNHCR or whichever organisation that needed clearance to get into the enclave. And all we needed to do was to write a letter to the BSA or make a call through Mr. Petar and then they will say whether they are going to grant the permission or not. It was that easy. It didn't have to take a whole day, it didn't have to take a whole week. So -- and also if I go further to the escort bit that you mentioned. This could have been coupled with our normal patrols. We could organise that because we knew when the crossing was to take place and we just send one patrol to go and escort this convoy or these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: An unarmed patrol; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unarmed in terms of guns, in terms of other weapons, but armed with a pen and a book and a bit of intelligence and a bit of negotiation skills that could enable us penetrate each and every area, even most of the time the heavily guarded ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, I am aware that the civilian affairs department communicated with us, I'm aware of letters from them and information which they sent to me, I have plenty of them as well as the Main Staff, also the UNPROFOR. I am aware that the UNPROFOR also had an armed escort for the convoys and that we would approve the convoys, the Main Staff as well as the committee in charge of approving that would approve the requests from those organisations, UN agencies, and we never received a single request from the military observers that would refer to somebody else other than military observers. Where did you send requests for convoys to be approved, to whom did you send them?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were sending them through the normal BSA channels. We would write to the BSA through Major Nikolic. Whether it ended up there, we did not know. All we know is we could get clearance and we could be able to escort these people in to the enclave. Also, there is the normal clearance that the convoy would ask through the BSA. And at times they would be compelled to disclose what they were bringing in and they write everything, whatever is inside there. But they also copy the same to us and tell us, "Please come and escort us" from a certain place, which we would readily do. At times they would request the UNPROFOR, that is, the DutchBat in Srebrenica, to go and escort them. So it could be either way, but for sure we used to provide these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the task of UNPROFOR in relation to convoys if you did this?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that question would be better answered by UNPROFOR, because they had their own mandate, their own roles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 9 you say that DutchBat was not duty-bound to inform you about anything. There was no system of exchange of information, but from time to time you did exchange information. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you could only know what the six of you had seen and what DutchBat wanted you to know; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right. There are so many sources of information. If you read the whole thing, you see we had so many sources of information. And one of them being local information, that is, information from the local people. We could get information from DutchBat officially. We could also get information from their observation posts because we had a free hand of going there to observe the situation from there. And we could get a write-up, intelligence write-up, from our headquarters, gathered and maybe sent to us for further verification. And we could also get information through the BSA when we held meetings with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, I would like to ask you kindly to focus on what you say in paragraph 9. [In English] "There was no system whereby they were or ought to have told us about the military activities both inside and outside." [Interpretation] This is what I'm interested in now. Did one person go out on patrol or two or three?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it depended on the situation, in that at times we could have more people in the enclave, at times and especially during the onslaught on the enclave we had reduced personnel, we had only two, so the number in a patrol would differ. But normally we were to have two UNMOs and one interpreter in one patrol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, Colonel, sir, do you have your amalgamated statement with you now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot access it right now, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about providing him a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm putting these questions because I want to deal with your position on the demilitarisation of Srebrenica and the military presence there in the enclave as well as the presence of weaponry. Because your views drastically differ from the views of other UN institutions, going all the way up to the Secretary-General himself. Did you know that the Secretary-General had said that protected areas are armed strongholds of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not understand that, Your Honour. Maybe you can ask it differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here comes the question. Do you have any explanation in view of the following? How come you believe that there were no troops there, no weapons, that there were no military operations undertaken by the 28th Division of the Muslim army, whereas everybody else in the UN is saying something different? I'm not accusing the observers. I'm just saying that perhaps they didn't inform you about this. Now, this is what I'm interested in: Do you simply not know about this or do you assert that no such thing happened there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you're talking about the military activities in Srebrenica, one thing that is certain is that what was on the Muslim side was minimal. Definitely there were small arms and we have reported about them, there were some -- even some machine-guns and we reported seeing people armed with machine-guns. Those reports are there. But obviously you cannot compare that kind of weaponry with what was on the BSA side. This is exactly what I mean by the statement you have referred to, in that the -- the BSA side had heavy artillery. They had tanks. They had other weapons like heavy machine-guns. They had rocket-launchers, which we have all documented. They had all the heavy weapons that any army has. They had everything. So it's in comparison with that, that is where we are saying really there was nothing much that we could see from the Muslim side. Because although they had those small arms, really they could not be able to encounter the heavy weaponry that was with the other side. Secondly, the issue of demilitarisation. When we went in there, when I personally went in there, I found it had already been concluded, it was done a lot -- much earlier. But obviously there were some small arms which were left. That is obvious. We -- I cannot deny that. But then the issue of having a protected area by the UN was because those who were inside there have already given up their arms and they need protection of the UN from attacks by the armed groups that were around them. That was the main aim of having a UN protected area, that those who were inside, you don't have anything that can be able to attack these other people outside. And so the people outside do not have a reason to come and bombard you in your area. That was the main reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please focus on paragraph 15 of your statement, where you say, I'm going to read it out in English. [In English] "I was asked whether the cease-fire violations included holding or keeping military units inside the enclave. The violations to the cease-fire agreement were several. One of them was that no one should be able to have arms inside the safe area, and that is why all the Muslims were disarmed and all the heavy weapons and small arms, machine-guns, and all that were taken to a safe place, that is, the DutchBat compound. This was happening in all other demilitarised areas, not just Srebrenica." [Interpretation] Do you agree that there were six protected areas that had been declared by the United Nations? Let me help you with this. I'm going to enumerate them, Srebrenica, Zepa, Sarajevo, Maglaj or Mostar, and then there is Bihac out there, and Tuzla. Right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, but you've forgotten Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And Gorazde too. Are these protected areas? And what about paragraph 15, does it not say that Srebrenica was demilitarised and unarmed and that all the others were protected areas too?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Really what you are saying is what is written. I don't get your question on the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that all six protected areas were demilitarised and disarmed?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would request that though we are going to -- though you are looking at all the other UN protected areas, we focus mainly our attention on Srebrenica because that is the point at hand. So the other areas we can just mention them in passing and say that they were UNPAs, that is, UN protected areas, and they expected the same that was happening in Srebrenica to be happening in those other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But you mentioned that this pattern, namely, demilitarisation, surrender of weapons, seizure of weapons was the same in Srebrenica and in all other six -- no, five protected zones. So you brought in the others; it wasn't me. That is why we have to clarify whether that was actually the case.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I still stand by what I've said. Let's have a reference on Srebrenica. The mention of these other areas was in that it was expected to be the same all over, but obviously different areas it differed. So as far as I know, Srebrenica was not in isolation as a UN protected area, and I expected all the others to have been the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. So that was your wish and your expectation. However, here it is presented like an assertion and you have to understand the Defence, we have to see what reality was as distinguished from your wishful thinking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Then let us dwell on Srebrenica only. Mr. Kingori, do you claim that Srebrenica was demilitarised and that all the weapons there had been seized? That is what it seems to be like on the basis of this paragraph, but today you said that there were some side arms there and even machine-guns. Or did you say that they did not have any machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I said is that demilitarisation had already been done in the whole enclave. All the heavy weapons were put in Bravo Company of DutchBat, and when I went in there I was shown where those heavy weapons were. And most of the other small arms had been collected and put in that same safe area. So as far as I was concerned, demilitarisation had already been done. But I also added that you could not miss a few small arms out there which had not been collected. That is normal in any area. So that's exactly what I said and I still believe that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I say, Mr. Kingori, that the Muslims themselves left their documents and that they had handed over only weapons that did not work and if I say to you that you said somewhere, perhaps during the interview, that you as observers did not check how usable the weapons that had been handed over were, what would you say to that? I'm holding Naser Oric's interview in my hands and he says: "We handed over only weapons that were not in order and all the rest we kept." Did they deceive you successfully?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I know for sure is that the weapons were handed over and you could see them in the Bravo Company. But also, we were not checking the serviceability state of those weapons. Anyone's -- any other person's assertion that maybe only the unserviceable ones were handed over really is their own -- they are the ones who said that, not me. What I know is that it was done under the UN watch and those weapons were given to DutchBat so that they could be able to take care of them and also ensure that nobody goes in there to pick them. In any war, for sure, propaganda, is very important. So somebody can say, "We all have the important weapons." After all, in war you can say you have the biggest army, the best army. That does not necessarily have to translate to the actual truth. You could have a different situation on ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, do we agree that Naser Oric was the commander of the 28th Division, the 28th Srebrenica Division, and that he was the number one man of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, as mentioned in my statement somewhere is that this is a person I never met, Naser Oric, but we were told was the head of the Muslim establishment in the enclave. But he's a person I never met. He's a person we had scanty details about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you said that in your view the demilitarisation of Srebrenica had been carried out a lot before you arrived there, are you trying to say that it took place in May or the summer of 1993 when the agreement on demilitarisation had been reached?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not trying to say that. I'm just trying to say it was done much earlier before I arrived there. As to the dates, I don't know, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, the -- can I ask the connotation of the statement that demilitarisation had already been done before you arrived there. Does it mean that the weapons had been taken before you arrived and you didn't investigate into whether there are further weapons inside the enclave yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the demilitarisation of the whole of former Yugoslavia was done much, much earlier, and especially I think -- I tend to think it was done during the peace agreement or immediately after the peace agreement. I think that was somewhere in 1993. So thereafter is when they had agreed -- after they had agreed that some areas needed to be demilitarised so that they can be protected by the UN, that's when the demilitarisation process was done. But as to the dates when it was done, I'm not very sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My point was whether the demilitarisation itself is not something that should be done in a continuous or constant basis, not at certain point of time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, demilitarisation was done at once. But continuously, if later on you find that some people are still armed, you could go in and remove those weapons from them. But that is not the main demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we briefly look at D1967. Could we please have that in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Could I please ask you to identify this. Tell us, is this a report dated the 17th of February, 1995, about received weapons at the command of the 8th Operations Group in Srebrenica? Just look at the quantities involved, mortar shells, explosives, bullets, and so on. Were you aware of that? Would you have considered this to be demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can see all this and for sure this does not mean that demilitarisation had not been done. This can be called re-arming, but at the same time you could see the kind of equipments which are said to have been brought in. We are talking about small arms, cigarettes, salt, yeah, some communication equipments, rocket-propelled guns, you know, grenades, that is 7-2 rockets. And bring your attention to the fact that, yes, I can see this. But you're just seeing the mortars which are how many? I think they are 60-millimetre mortars, mortar shells. And really you can see there these are 77.9-millimetre bullets or these -- they may look much to somebody who does not know how an army operates, they may look much, but seriously this is nothing to wage war with. This is practically nothing. If you compare with what we know, and I know you cannot bring that up here, that was in the hands of the BSA, really this is peanuts. This is nothing. We are talking about, what, two RPG rockets, 7.62 millimetres, that's small arms. So mortars are how many, six? Six mortars are for a section -- no, not even a company. It's a platoon. So this cannot be compared at all with what the BSA had. Even if they had double this, this cannot be compared with what the BSA had. It's nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But, Mr. Kingori, tell me, you described this as re-arming, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said it could not have been -- it does not mean that demilitarisation had not been done. It only means that they had requested for re-arming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bringing in some more arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But would you have been aware of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we were not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree, Mr. Kingori, that this had been submitted on the 17th of February and that that does not mean that that had not been there already. Could Mr. Kingori please be shown the second page, where we can see that mortars are being requested, or rather, mortar shells for an 82-millimetre mortar. And also ammunition for tanks. If I were to tell you that they had three tanks in this demilitarised protected zone, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say I did not know if they had the three tanks at all. We were not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see this here, that he's asking for 82-millimetre mortar shells, 60-millimetre mortar shells, and 100-millimetre tank shells; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have a look at 1D04730.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have not agreed that you were aware of the existence of the 28th Division consisting of five brigades and a few independent battalions in Srebrenica. Did you come to realise after our interview that that was true after all? Had you known about that and had you forgotten in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not know of the existence of such a brigade, such a heavy organisation, I was not aware about it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, what did the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina have in the enclave? What kind of infrastructure, what kind of structure, how many combatants, how many units? Not the brigade. I'm talking about the division, the 28th Division, consisting of five brigades, including one in Zepa. I'm asking you about what you knew and about what -- and on the basis of what you drew conclusions about the conduct of both sides. To the best of your knowledge, what did the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina have in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, all we knew about the BiH was that they had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, are you hearing the answer of the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- is that they had some structures which we cannot call organisations as such, because at least we knew there was a Chief of Staff, who was Ramiz Becirovic, and that there was a military leader that was called Naser Oric, who we never met during our stay in Srebrenica. But about how they were organised, we did not know, because for sure a division -- you cannot have somebody in charge of a division that could not be seen. By that I mean the -- the 28th Division that is always talked about could have been there in existence or on paper as a division, but in reality you could not have had a division in such an enclave as Srebrenica. You could not have had in any ordinary or conventional military, you cannot have that. And I will draw your attention, Your Honours, to the fact that a division is broken down to various organisations in that in a military we start with a section which is composed of nine people. That is a section. It is the first fighting unit, the smallest fighting unit. Three sections form a platoon. Three platoons form a company. And three companies ordinarily form a unit. We are talking about a unit now has got about 1.000 people. It's not just the personnel, but that is the point I would like you to note. Sorry, Your Honour. It's not just the personnel but the accompanying weaponry, in that a section just has small arms. If you go to a platoon, they start getting a mortar, one mortar. It goes on like that until you get heavy-support weapons. And that could not be seen in the enclave. There was not such a structure. Even if, as he says, there could have been a tank, two, or three, that is actually to support what, a division? A division is supposed to have two tank battalions. It's supposed to be supported by two tank battalions. It was not there. You could not see that. Even if you are talking about a whole division, a whole division is the next to an army, it is not easy to hold such a big number of personnel in such a small enclave. Secondly, hold those heavy weapons without being seen, all of them in such an enclave, very small area. Your Honour, it's practically impossible, practically impossible. Thirdly, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that for such a military to continue, there has got to be training, continuous training, which is not evident anywhere. During our -- it was not evident during our stay in Srebrenica, nor is it noted anywhere that I know of the continuous training. It was not there. So what I'm trying to drive at is the division could have been there in writing, but in reality on ground there was nothing to show that there was such a division in Srebrenica, and in fact it could not have been there as a division with the personnel and the heavy weaponry. It's not possible, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, let us distinguish between two things. First you said you didn't see it and you don't know it, and then you say it did not exist. What exactly is your position, you didn't know about it, although it may have existed, or it did not exist at all? Is it one or the other?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, my answer remains the same, that the division -- we did not see the division, though we knew there was a Chief of Staff to a division. But in reality there was no division as such. Secondly, even if it could have been there, there was no evidence to it being there on ground. As a military person, really there was nothing to show for a division in that place. And like what we had on the BSA side, you could see the kind of weaponry they had. Their structures that they had is quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this opinion of yours shared by the other five military observers?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, as a senior military officer, I knew that is how it was and I believe the other observers that we had shared the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the Dutch Battalion have the same view as the one you just expressed? Did they share your position?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the view of DutchBat I may be unable to talk about because they had their own way of operating. But one thing I know for sure is that they could not see a division, a whole infantry division, operating inside Srebrenica. They could not have seen that other than maybe in words, somebody saying or whatever, but not an infantry division in Srebrenica. I'm sure they could not have seen that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you then explain this to us. If you did not inform the Secretary-General that Srebrenica is a military stronghold of the BH army, if the Dutch Battalion did not do that or the Canadian Battalion before them, then who deceived the Secretary-General and led him to inform the Security Council that the protected areas --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- were strongholds of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- it's not for the witness to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the document you see on the screen. Do you see this is the 2nd of June, 1995, when you were there. Look at all the things that have to be distributed in terms of military assets. Ammunition, 5500, 350 for an old rifle, grenades to the 280th Brigade, 281st, 282nd, 283rd, 284th, and 280th Mountain Battalion. The Zepa Brigade is not mentioned here. Then on the next page you can see a staff unit, et cetera, a huge amount of ammunition. How come a brigade that does not exist uses so much ammunition? And this is a request for June 1995. It's obvious that they had used up what they had before. How does this tally with your reporting as a military observer that there was nothing there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to see the whole document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who issued it? It's on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a certification that this is authentic -- oh, yes, you are right, you can see at the top, Semsudin Salihovic, Semso. In the original there is a stamp, the command of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour -- yeah, I can see this. Maybe you can take me back to the second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Your Honour, you can see -- I can see all this. I can see the type of weaponry being requested, or rather, they're saying they have provided. And you can see some bullets, 7.62-millimetres, 60-millimetres, rocket-launchers. Yeah, I can see all this. And I would draw your attention to the fact that this is what was said to have been provided for the BiH in the enclave. If that is what was provided, really I cannot deny that. All I know is that I did not know about the existence of this or the supply of this kind of weaponry, but also if you look at the kind of weaponry that is being provided, really it's not much. The heaviest is a 60-millimetre hand-held rocket-launcher, which are two. Yeah. There's another one, that makes them three. So if you look at all the others, about 80 per cent we are talking about, the small arms bullets, that is 7.62, 7.9-millimetre bullet, which are small arms. So we are talking about small -- a small arms. Majority of this is for small arms. That is what can be seen. But the only medium weapon is the 60-millimetre mortar, that is the only thing that can be seen here. One other thing to note is that there is no heavy weaponry. There are no artillery shells. I cannot see any artillery shells. So in essence, this is not for heavy weaponry. It's not for heavy artillery at all. So this still confirms of what I had said earlier, that it could have been said there was a division inside there, but as for the support arms, really it's not there, even with all this. There's no evidence of an infantry division in the enclave. It could have been there in writing, it could have been there, even in a few -- a few personnel could have been there. They could have called themselves whatever. But really, there is no evidence of such an existence. And obviously the point to note here is that this resupply, this resupply, because I can call it resupply because they're being told, We are sending you this, it essentially means they had reached a point whereby they needed to support their people. I mean, this could have been coming from outside the enclave. That's what I believe because they're saying, We are sending you this. It could not have been coming from inside the enclave. I don't believe it was coming from inside the enclave, but if that is what happened I would say I was not privy to this information but draw your attention to the fact that this is a resupply to or of small arms, not of the heavy weaponry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Colonel, could you expand on what you said, i.e., this: "... they had reached a point whereby they needed to support their people." What did you mean, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By this, Your Honour, I mean the logistics person who has signed this, who is calling himself brigadier something, I saw it at the signature block, really wanted to resupply or to rearm the people inside the enclave. And to me what that means is that this could not have been coming from inside the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: One second. Could it also mean, Colonel, that they would have had arms and ammunition before and they're now seeking additional or a resupply of those arms and ammunition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, what this means is that whoever is sending this knows that whatever is inside there, meaning there must have been something. And that is why, and it is in our reports, we could see there was small arms fire from time to time, meaning they were expending whatever they had. So they had to be resupplied. All this is in our reports. It's not that the whole place had no gun at all and I've said that earlier. They had small arms. They were firing -- in fact, normal firing in Srebrenica. It was a normal thing. If you stay for one night, two nights without any small arms fire, you feel that there is something which is not very right, in quotes. But what I mean here is whoever is trying to send this feels that the people inside there do not have enough and that is why they had to be supplied with this, meaning that the supply is not coming from within, it's not coming from inside the enclave. It's coming from somewhere outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, this says clearly that this comes from the staff of the 28th Division. Semsudin Salihovic, on the authorisation of Commander Oric, who is temporarily absent, ordered that these four brigades and these battalions be given from the depot a replenishment of combat sets for all these weapons. This came a long time ago illegally to their depot and is being distributed from the depot. Doesn't this say clearly that there are four brigades to which this ammunition is allocated? And I would appreciate yes or no answers whenever possible because we don't have enough time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the witness answered that question. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, can we agree that a demilitarised protected area must not and should not contain any armed units except police with small weapons, side arms.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, a demilitarised area ideally should have no weaponry at all, no weapons at all. But you find in this case - and we documented that - we could see some people who were armed moving about in the enclave, we could see that, and we could report on the same so that something could be done about it. And at one time the DutchBat also noted that and told a meeting that we had with the Chief of Staff, Ramiz Becirovic, to make sure that the people hand over their weapons. He asked them, "Why are your soldiers still moving about with weapons?" Because ideally they're not supposed to be armed at all. But I said and I may be forced to repeat this, that though they were disarmed, the disarmament had already been done, demilitarisation had already been done, you could find a few people with arms. That was evident and we were reporting on the same. But that does not mean that the whole enclave was militarised because obviously it could have presented a very different scenario if the whole enclave was allowed to have proper militarisation, the way it was before the demilitarisation was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, are you aware that the State Security Service of Bosnia-Herzegovina reported on the 17th or 18th of July from Tuzla that 10.000 fighting men of the 28th Division made a breakout, a military armed breakout, through the Serb territory?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You would like to see the reference?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will show it after the break, Your Excellency. I just want to know if Mr. Kingori was aware that in addition to those captured and those dead, 10.000 fighting men made it alive to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Or you didn't know that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not know -- I do not know how many made it to Tuzla -- in fact, up to now I don't have that figure. And also hasten to add when you say "fighting men," it may be ordinary people with arms not necessarily soldiers. So maybe you can show us the qualification, whether they were actually soldiers or just people carrying arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What distinction do you make between a person carrying and using a weapon and a soldier? Don't both kill equally?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we may not have dwell on this, but for sure anybody with a gun can kill, anybody with a gun is dangerous, but obviously we know there's more to handling a weapon than just holding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you informed, Mr. Kingori, that those people whom you called armed non-soldiers had killed over 3.000 Serbs around Srebrenica and that, day and night, all the time, they went out into Serb territory and killed. And 2.000 of them got killed in Serb territory before July 1995, not in Srebrenica but in Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I can say for sure is that when we used to hold meetings with the BSA, we could hear some complaints about the Serb -- the Muslims having crossed through the Serb territory to and from Zepa to bring goods. And at times they would be attacked, they would be injured. We could also hear of some Muslims attacking some BSA, but we never heard about any BSA having been killed by the Muslims at all. We were never informed of any BSA soldiers who had been killed by the Muslims at all in all the meetings that we held with the BSA. But on the other hand, we could be told by the Muslims of several number of their people having been killed by the BSA. So by that I mean there was killing of the Muslims by the BSA and not vice versa. But of course, you cannot discount one or two anywhere, but we never documented anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Excellent.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this previous document be admitted before I call another one before the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit 1D4730.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1993, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: During the interview, and I believe earlier today, you implied that you were not aware of various military staffs and the military infrastructure in Srebrenica itself. If the soldiers could have been around the periphery and in their own homes and you were unable to see them, do you still stand by your assertion there were no military staffs in Srebrenica itself?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I still do in that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 1D4769. I believe this should be 1994 because we had 1993 yesterday. The previous should have a higher number, a higher exhibit number, 1994, but perhaps I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have a look, Mr. Kingori. This is dated 22nd February 1995. The National Defence Secretariat Tuzla, a branch of the Ministry of Defence, replies enumerating all the assets they have. The command of the 8th Operations Group is located in the Lovac feature in old town, Stari Grad. And they also have a total area of 198 square metres. The old staff of the Territorial Defence of Srebrenica is used by the command of the place. Total area, et cetera, et cetera. For every brigade, 280th Brigade is located in a family house of Meho Hrvacic. The 281st is placed in a family house owned by Hajro Dautbasic -- no, that's all one brigade. And then are listed 281st, 282nd, 283rd --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- 284th Brigade. They have all the command posts, they have staff headquarters, they have staff units, they have an independent 7th Mountain Battalion. Srebrenica is crawling with troops and military infrastructure and you are saying that was not so. And the Dutch Battalion is aware of this, but the military observers are not.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I look at the whole of this list and draw you back to what I said earlier, that you really cannot have a brigade being housed in a house, in one house, the way you have seen house belonging to a certain lady here that is holding a brigade. Really, a brigade comprises of 3 -- minimum --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Not brigade, sir --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- there is somewhere where a brigade headquarters is given as a house. And for your information, a brigade cannot be housed in such a place. It is difficult. It's impossible. A brigade has got three infantry units, and a whole unit, actually, can occupy the whole of Srebrenica in normal circumstances. In fact, Srebrenica was just a village. That should have been actually for a company, not more than a company. Then you look at the heavy weapons that support a brigade. So even if we look at all this written down, it looks very nice, house Podgaj used by - that is number 5 - by the 3rd LPC owned by Ibrahim whoever. You can see even the area, 55 square metres. That is very small area. It's not even for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That purpose was army kitchen, it says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does it not say that house was used as a kitchen, number 5?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It does not say that it holds a whole company or unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but for 55 -- I'm looking at the 55 square metres even for a kitchen for even a brigade or even a company. Later on -- even if it is a platoon, a platoon cannot be -- you cannot have a kitchen for a platoon in such a small area. The attention I'm trying to bring in here is that it -- you can say that -- it can be said that this is what they had. That is fine. But in reality, this is not easy to hold. You cannot have a brigade -- a whole brigade, a whole division in such a small area being scattered in these small, small houses. Where is even the control and command? In these small, small houses, if one is put here, the other one is put there, the other one is put in another place, it cannot work. It cannot work. Hence my earlier assertion that this could have just been on paper or an assumption, fine. You could have had a few soldiers. I'm not denying that. The soldiers were there, a few soldiers were there. We had -- they even had the small arms, fine. But really, you cannot have a whole division distributed like this in such a small enclave. It really cannot work, and I don't believe it could have been the same even on the BSA side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, please. You as a military observer were supposed to determine that that army is not properly in barracks. The troops live at home and when they are on the defence line then food is prepared for them in the kitchen. This does not say that these houses were barracks for the whole brigade or battalion. They were just staff headquarters housing commanders and their staff. You see, for instance, the 282nd Brigade was in a hotel, hotel called Domavija and so on. So let's not create a confusion. If you draw your conclusions thinking of a professional army living in barracks, then it's something different. But here we are dealing with soldiers who live in their homes, not in barracks, and they take shifts going to the front line or into various operations, carrying out missions. Wasn't it your duty to know what kind of army you're dealing with?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I knew the kind of army. I knew the kind of military disposition that was in that area, and not just me, all the military observers that were there. But for sure the kind of military people that we had there, the BiH side really were not, and I still maintain, an army that you could have called a conventional army. It does not matter whether the army is staying -- is going for patrols and coming back and just being cooked for in a certain house or whatever. There are procedures even in war that are followed. There are ways that you must -- you can show that here we have a military organisation and you have seen that even in other wars. Even when we had the Afghanistan issue, when we had the Iraq issue, we could see that this is a military organisation in certain place. There are certain procedures, minimum issues that have got to be observed. But when you look at the dispensation that we are getting here, this is quite a disorganised military, if it was a military at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- admit this document as Exhibit D1994. We will take a break for half an hour after which I expect you to move on to your next topic. We'll resume at five past --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like you just to consider giving me more time because Mr. Kingori is giving quite detailed answers which, of course, can be useful to us but it will leave many topics uncovered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just concentrate on important issues and be focused. We'll resume at five past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Please may I ask just for indulgence for a few minutes -- few seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, did you know how much of the humanitarian aid food was going to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Srebrenica, to the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not know of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It seems that this has not been uploaded into e-court, but it does have a 1D number. Perhaps this can then wait for a little bit. You were already asked about this, Mr. Kingori. Do you know that the 28th Division intending to help the Muslim offensive in Sarajevo which began on the 15th of June, 1995, that they conducted quite powerful assault activities around Srebrenica in order to tie-up and prevent the Serbian army from going to the aid of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Speaking about the things that you were able to do, you agreed that you did not have access to an entire quadrant, an entire sector, of the Srebrenica zone, the so-called Bandera Triangle. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: During the interview you described to us that you would be stopped by armed men. Do you know that in the same way the armed soldiers of DutchBat were stopped?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm aware of that and it is on record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If we're talking about tanks, then you don't know -- actually, it's possible that they could have had three tanks in the Bandera Triangle without you knowing that. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For sure. It was very easy for me to not know. But at the same time, such information could have sort of filtered to our direction and we could have known if the tanks were there. But for sure there is a possibility they could have been there without our knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is all that I would like to establish, Mr. Kingori, whether there was something that you were not able to report on because you didn't have access to the information or didn't know it. This is what I would like to establish. This is what I would like to establish. And now the attacks from the enclave in the second half of June were so intense so that the Serbs had a lot of casualties around Srebrenica. For example, the Serbian village of Visnjica was burned and civilians there were killed on the 26th of June.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I start with the issue of us not getting access to some information, for sure like Bandera Triangle we could not be able to access, there was a restriction of movement, which we complained about. And for the casualties you are talking about of Serbs, I may not be aware of that. There is -- that of Serbian village of Visnjica, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D04780.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Did you complete your answer, Colonel? I noted that you were waiting for the consultation between Mr. Karadzic and his legal advisor be completed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is what I was waiting for. But for sure I think the answer is complete. We can continue, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D04780, please. There should be a translation. Perhaps there isn't one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In that case I will read the document to you. This is a document from the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina of the 27th of June. If you can look at the section for 9.45, where it says: "In the morning on the 26th of June, 1995, our forces from the Srebrenica sector attacked and torched the village of Visnjica. The Chetniks did have casualties among the civilian population." And then for 9.48 it states: "The Chetniks have information about the infiltration of a number of our groups from Zepa moving towards Kladanj and are taking all available measures for combat in such conditions, and all the units in the -- in that sector have been alerted to the first degree of combat-readiness." So this is a little bit outside of your sector where a fierce war is waging in which the Muslims are attacking and the Serbs are defending their territory. This is on the evening of the 26th of June. Is that correct, Mr. Kingori?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can see -- I have listened to what you have said and, for sure, this never appeared in any of the meetings that we held with the BSA who could have, in normal circumstances, complained about such an issue. So we were not -- it was not brought to our attention at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this. We can mark it for identification and then we will ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, did you know that David Harland reported about the casualties among the civilians and that the UN and other organisations were informed about it and they did have that information?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For sure we did not get this information and my worry is why even on the BSA side there were no complaints lodged with us on this issue if it ever happened, because normally they would tell us to complain to the BiH that they did this and that. And on this occasion there was no such a complaint from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West, do you have any objection to the admission of this document, separate from marking it for identification?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1995, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now ask to have P2284, please, and it would be paragraph 225. So this is a Prosecution exhibit, 2284, and in the document it would be paragraph 225. Paragraph 225 in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a report by the UN Secretary-General; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we zoom in on paragraph 225, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It states here, I don't have to read it: [In English] "... a raiding party of Bosniaks under the leadership of Zulfo Tursunovic attacked the Serb village of Visnjica, 5 kilometres west of the western edge of the Srebrenica enclave. During the attack in the early morning of 26th of June, several houses were burned, and either two people were killed, according to Bosniak sources, or four, according to Serb sources. (Approximately 100 sheep were also stolen and taken back to Srebrenica, where they were subsequently eaten)." [Interpretation] So the United Nations knew about that. And you can look further down. [In English] "... the attack, although relatively minor in comparison to the Serb attacks which preceded it, led to strong Serb condemnations. Serb army spokesman Milutinovic stated that it was the job of UNPROFOR to prevent such operations, and that the attack therefore demonstrated that 'the United Nations forces are aligning themselves with the Muslim army.' General Mladic stated to UNPROFOR that Bosniak attacks from Srebrenica 'brutally violate the status of the safe area of Srebrenica. Due to that fact, I strongly protest and warn you that we will not tolerate such cases in the future.' Mladic failed to mention what UNPROFOR [sic] had reported to United Nations ..." and so on. [Interpretation] When you speak about your information and when you talk about protests from the Serbian side, did the Army of Republika Srpska submit their protests to the observers or to UNPROFOR? And this is where we come to the question of what exactly your mandate was.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the protest could have gone to any of the UN agencies there. In fact, the Bosnian Serbs should have complained to us, but if they complained to UNPROFOR, that is, the DutchBat which was there in that particular moment, there was nothing wrong with that, only that it was not brought to our attention. But provided they have complained to any UN agency, I don't think there was anything wrong with that. And for us not knowing about it, there are also some things we knew that UNPROFOR did not know. So these things used to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But, Colonel, what I am having a bit of problem in grasping is this: You weren't aware of this situation at all, you say. Did you not say so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was not aware about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Now, here we have the report of the Secretary-General referring to this situation. Are you in a position at all to explain to us this severe disconnect between your -- you and the Secretary-General, between UNMO and the S-G?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the UN systems have got different ways of getting information. They have different ways. They could have gotten information through us, that is, the UNMOs; they could have gotten information through UNPROFOR; there were other aid agencies like UNHCR, IOM, and other agencies who could have channelled such information without necessarily referring to us. So the UN system had different ways of getting information. So they could have gotten it through any other channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, this is what is causing my concern. In your statement there are some assertions, even detailed descriptions of certain situations, the position of the Army of Republika Srpska and so on and so forth. However, all this was drafted with a major lack of information on your part. There is confusion between how we viewed the MOs and how you viewed them. I claim that the military observers were not the party to whom we submitted our protests nor did we expect six unarmed persons to intervene. According to our understanding, you were passive observers who were reporting back to the United Nations, nothing more than that. But you understood your role differently and it's evident actually that a lot of information bypassed you. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not correct at all. For one, the military observers were the ears and eyes of the UN on the ground, and especially on issues to do with military activities inside the enclave. But as I said, the UN had different systems of getting information. Some of this information could have been sent back again to us for verification or for confirmation. But if not, definitely there were areas through which the UN could get and verify such information. As military observers our role was very distinct and we did it to the best of our ability, given the circumstances. And you cannot correctly say that us being six could have limited our capabilities, could have diminished our capabilities. What I know is that six unarmed military observers was a normal force deployed in any sector, in any team. That was the normal composition in a team. And definitely you don't want us to believe that the UN did not know what they were doing. With six military observers, two who could form a patrol, we had at least two operational patrols that could be sent out at any given time. Of course the other two could be left manning the area and doing normal domestics. But then with two patrols you could be able to penetrate each and every area of the enclave as part of the plan that we had. It was not every day that we had to patrol. There were scheduled meetings with both sides, both the BSA and the BiH, which we had to go for. And this is where we were exchanging information with either side. That is, like this issue, the BSA should have brought it in one of the scheduled meetings, which they did not bring up at that particular time. So you cannot just say that the UN -- there was a disconnect because the UN has written about the -- the UN Secretary-General has written about this and General Mladic has written about it, but at the same time failed to recognise that even the BSA -- the local BSA command should have complained about it to us and they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, can -- well, we can agree that you were the ears and the eyes of the United Nations. But you also have this idea that you were also its legs and arms and that your task was action. However, the Army of Republika Srpska did not receive nor did it send its protests to you. They were sent to someone else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please look at 1D04786.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can see that this was sent regularly but not to you. It was addressed to the UNPROFOR. What I'm concerned about now is how to view and what to do with your assertions stated in 200-plus paragraphs, stating that you were denied a lot of information or that you were not even supposed to have this information because of the nature of your mandate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There should be a translation of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, can you please look to the UNPROFOR in the enclave Srebrenica. When you speak about the UN, I agree. But you're talking from the position of a military observer, not from the position of the United Nations. And you can see this protest by General Zivanovic of the 20th of March, 1995, about the behaviour of Muslim formations which could not be tolerated. Did you know about this? You were there already at the time.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will start with the first question on why this was sent to the UNPROFOR and reiterate that their mandate was slightly different from ours and you know that and I've already said that before, in that they were armed and they could enforce peace in that particular area. We were not there to enforce peace but to observe. That is where some of these issues like where he has said: "... we cannot tolerate Muslim formations obstinately leaving the enclave and attacking areas out of the enclave borders," and said that something should be done. Really, the UNPROFOR had the arms to do that. We did not have the arms to do that and we were not expected to do that because that was not part of our mandate. Ours was to write about these incidents when they occurred and send them to the UN headquarters through the normal channels. But for this, obviously we were not expected to enforce.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, again we come to the question of the mandate, the assignment. How was your task defined, in what document? Because here the Army of Republika Srpska has intensive memorandums and contacts with UNPROFOR. The observers are the eyes and ears and not the arms and legs. It is not in their mandate, in the way we understand it, any authorisation or was it their task to undertake any actions. Their task was just to observe and to report. How is this different from the way in which you understood your assignment?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wish the same question could have been asked to Major Nikolic or Colonel Vukovic, who knew what our roles were in that enclave and who used us throughout our stay in the enclave in terms of giving us information on what was happening and guiding -- telling us what should be done by the UN and we were reporting on the same. And also giving us a view of what they were intending to do because I wonder why if the observers were not important in that area, why Colonel Vukovic could tell us of what they were planning to do. Like when they were planning to take over the enclave, he told us in his own record. Why would he tell us that if he thought the UNMOs had no purpose in that area? Really, we had our own mission and we did it to the best of our ability. But when it comes to armed issues, there was -- the UNPROFOR could have -- maybe the BSA felt they were the ones who could deal with it so they channelled it, according to them, to the right people who could do that. But that does not mean we had no mandate -- we had no clear mandate. We had ours, and we were doing it to the best of our ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid that there's a lack of understanding here, but let us leave this aside. We'll have to find a document of the United Nations that defined your work. Mr. Kingori, as you said to us during the interview, you met with local officers of the Serb army and you socialised with them. Sometimes you would have a cup of coffee with them or something else and you also had some meetings. Did anyone keep minutes at these meetings when they informed you about what you told us?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted, Excellency, this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1996, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the meetings that we had with Major Nikolic or Colonel Vukovic were all minuted and we sent the minutes of what we discussed to the UNMO headquarters any time we held meetings with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On your side who was it that kept the minutes of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are the ones, we were taking minutes. Whoever -- the observer who was there, one of them could take the minutes. And later on when we got to the -- to our headquarters write them, refine them, and also -- and send them to the UNMO headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
