utterances.text: Thank you. With all due respect to you personally and to Major Nikolic and Colonel Vukovic, are you the appropriate level to discuss these major strategic moves? What was it that you could decide on in that respect and generally discuss, unless you just mean chatting about this?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that question maybe could have gone directly to Colonel Vukovic because he's the one who brought it up. Ours was to take what he was telling us. I hasten to add that later on it proved to be very true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us leave this aside, what ultimately turned out to be the case, and let us leave analogies aside. What kind of group are the three of you? That's what I'm interested in. What is it that you can decide on? And how can you talk about such major issues -- but never mind, we can ask them about that too. In paragraph 20 of your amalgamated statement you say that Muslims from Srebrenica went to Tuzla in order to get food. Do you know how large the Serb territory is there and how many Serb defence lines would have to be crossed on foot or on horseback in order to get to Tuzla and obtain food there? Do you have any idea how far away Tuzla is from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Tuzla was not very far from Srebrenica. But obviously it depends on what you mean by "far." What I know is that they used to go there. They were -- there was an organised way of requesting permission through the BSA. It was - and I've mentioned in my report - a mafia-type of operation where they would pay their way out and back to the enclave with the food and other items that they could buy from Tuzla. And then they bring them back into the enclave for sale. The -- at times when they did not honour this promise of payment, they would be ambushed and it's in our reports. Certain ambushes were being done because they had not delivered their bit of the promise. But for sure, whether it was far or near, they used to go there and bring goods to the enclave and we have evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I can believe that they brought food to the enclaves, but tell us how often did that happen?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the way, I need to correct something that was on the issue of Tuzla. Here what I mean was not Tuzla but Zepa. You may have to correct that. It is Zepa, not Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Aha. All right. Those 100 sheep that are mentioned in UN documents, were they brought from Zepa or Tuzla or Visnjica? And every time when they went out to the Serb villages to kill and torch, did they always bring some food from there? We know that they did that, but did you know?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, as for the hundred sheep, I don't think that question was asked in good faith because initially I had said I was not aware of that issue. So asking me whether they were brought in, you know, I don't know that. But anyway, it's okay. I was not aware of that so I cannot correctly comment on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that there was trade and food that they brought in different ways when they left the enclave. Did you know that we made offers to them to enable commercial traffic and transportation; however, the black marketeers who profited from such exercises did not allow that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, you would be the best person suited to tell us that. But on the mafia issue, the issue of people paying to get out and come back with goods, still remains.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have document 1D4971 to see what happened during May 1995 and how much humanitarian aid went to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the rural population around Srebrenica had their own households, livestock, and that they produced food for their own purposes at least and perhaps they had a bit of a surplus. Did you know that they kept livestock?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, there is a translation here. Please take a look at this report, Suljo Hasanovic is reporting to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina about the following. He says: "We hereby submit a list of the quantities of food, materiel, and technical equipment and fuel issued to our military units in our area for the month of May 1995. "25.900 kilogrammes of flour, 560 [as interpreted] kilogrammes of sugar, 1.423 litres of cooking oil, 619 kilogrammes of salt, 5.000 kilogrammes of beans, 17.000 cold cuts ..." Then powdered milk, fruit juice, and so on and so forth. And then further on it says: "We wish to note that the above quantities have been separated out of the humanitarian aid contingent which arrived in the area through UNHCR, while some of this food was obtained from the Dutch Battalion." So, sir, Mr. Kingori, if the Army of Republika Srpska is raising questions as to what is all of this food for, for Srebrenica I mean, when we know that the rural population has food of their own and we know that enormous amounts of food are being brought in, then we are being accused of discrimination, whereas we see here that an entire division was being fed here even by the Dutch Battalion. Even the Dutch Battalion allocated food for the army.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is not an issue that I would comfortably comment on because as for the UNHCR food, the normal UNHCR convoys were bringing food to the enclave because the people did not have enough food. They were mainly dependent on food from the UNHCR. That was the bottom line. Then on DutchBat, if they were giving any food to anybody else outside, I did not know. They never told us. They never recorded it with us. And I don't think it was in their mandate to supply food to the Muslim army. And UNHCR, if I go back to it, I would just say that there were no provisions -- I don't think there were any provisions for food to be given to the Muslim army. But of course when food is brought to the enclave for the entire population of the enclave, you could not miss maybe some food here and there finding its way to the military, either directly or indirectly, in that even some of the people who are enlisted and were also civilians in another way could get the food and give that to their soldiers. So I'm saying it is possible for the food to find its way to the military people, but there was no organised way of bringing in food through UNHCR to the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kingori. I'm not accusing any one of the UN agencies. I just wish to establish that accusations levelled against the Army of Republika Srpska in terms of them being restrictive are simply not true. These were months when the Army of Republika Srpska purportedly imposed restrictions. But look at this, tonnes and tonnes of food went to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was attacking us, killing us. And do you think that our intelligence people did not know that there was enough food there and that there was no need to feed the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and therefore these restrictions were justified? I'm not attacking anyone. I'm just saying that these accusations were false and unjustified. Do you agree that if in the month of May these hundreds of tonnes were being given to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to the 28th Division, somebody had to eat all of this, right? These tonnes of food, somebody had to eat all of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What question does he have to answer? One question at a time. But in any event, can you answer the question, Colonel? Is there any question at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, to me this looked like a statement that he's giving, so -- in fact, there is no answer but I can just expand on it and also seek to know if they -- there was food going to the soldiers, does it mean actually that everybody in the enclave was a soldier, so everybody got food. So in effect, having some food going to these soldiers does not mean that the enclave is full of food. The enclave was being fed by UNHCR. That is the way we knew. And even the harvest they were making, even planting some of their foodstuff that they were planting, was through assistance by UNHCR. And obviously there is no single time that we knew that the enclave was self-sufficient on food, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at paragraph 34 of your statement. I'm trying to put general questions and receive general answers because I do not have enough time for 207 paragraphs. So paragraph 34 you say that the situation in the enclave was serious and so on and so forth in respect of food. Also you refer to weekly reports and so on and so forth. In the meantime, in the month of May, out of the food that the Army of Republika Srpska is allowing to pass in order to provide it to the civilian population, this ultimately ends up with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that is waging war against us. Did you know about that, and would this paragraph 34 have been different had you known about that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were writing about how the situation was on ground as far as we knew it. And even now, if I were in the same circumstances, I would write the same because I knew for sure the enclave was not self-sufficient on food and we could go to some villages which had no food at all and we could write that in our reports. And the other monitoring agency, which was UNHCR, was also writing on the same, hence the request to send more food into the enclave. So the fact that you can see this list here does not necessarily mean that there was self-sufficiency of food in that enclave. In fact, there was a deficiency almost throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kingori, there wasn't enough food because the civilian population had been robbed. The food that was intended for the civilian population was sent to the army, whereas we were accused of imposing restrictions. Were we duty-bound to let the people feed the army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I think we heard the answer to that question from the witness. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1997, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D4972, please. Excellencies, I should be spending an equal amount of time in dealing with each and every paragraph of this statement if I am to challenge all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has to decide on all of this so I do need time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- we never cut off you from your cross-examination as long as you stick to relevant and important issues. Don't be repetitive in putting your question. I'm still of the opinion that you have sufficient time to cover all the issues. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This hasn't been translated yet, but there is no denying that this is a bulletin of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and of the military security service at that. The date is the 17th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. There is a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we put it on the ELMO or you can -- yes -- publish -- yes, let's put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the English version, the first and second paragraph specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that what it says here that: "Up until the 16th of July, 1995, in the early evening hours, approximately 10.000 members of the 28th Division arrived in the free territory as the main body of these forces were carrying out a breakthrough. The breakthrough was assisted by units of the 24th Division," which was not in Srebrenica but in Tuzla, "which launched a fierce counter-attack against the Chetnik lines in the Baljkovica sector (the general sector of Memici - Nezuk) and linked up with the units of the 28th Division ..." And then they say what their casualties were. 200 soldiers in one place, Konjevic Polje, and the Serbs had about 20 casualties and six captured, and so on and so forth. So is this something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Next page. Mr. Karadzic referred to first two paragraphs. When you're done with your reading, please let us know, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, is it clear to you now that your conclusions suffer from a lack of this particular information, that 10.000 managed to break through. Some were killed, others managed to get through. Do you realise now that your position that there were no troops there and that the 28th Division was only on paper is not accurate due to the lack of this particular information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see the first page again. Yes, Mr. Kingori.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, is there a place where they've put 10.000?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The first line --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first line, "approximately 10.000 members of the 28th Division ..." Your Honour, this is something that one cannot confirm or deny. But for sure, 10.000 soldiers is not a very small number. But who said these were all soldiers, these were trained soldiers? These were actually breaking out because they had been defeated and there were 10.000 armed soldiers. The reason why I'm saying this is that armed -- 10.000 armed soldiers are not just people with small arms. 10.000, we are talking about are close to a corps. If these cannot be able to break through in such a line, it is impossible, it is very difficult, if they are what we are calling armed. Armed, we are talking about they needed to have support arms. They could not just be soldiers because they have a gun. Soldiers are not soldiers just because they have a gun, no; they have small arms, no. It is obligatory that if it is a division like the one you are showing us here, 10.000 of them, that they have support arms. Where are their tanks? Where is the artillery? So in essence what I'm trying to say is these could be people with guns and that is possible to have. Anybody can have a gun. Anybody can pass through. He can also be called a soldier just because he has a gun. But in real sense, this is not an armed force because they lack the necessary capacity to be called an armed division.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, that is what worried me, because you keep saying this is logical, that is logical. However, we have to establish what actually happened irrespective of logic. So you are not challenging that this is a Muslim document that confirms that 10.000 soldiers left fighting their way along. Regardless of what is logical, this is a people's army. This is not a professional army. The Serb army and the Muslim armies were people's armies, not professional armies. People lived at home with their wives until they would leave. Are you challenging this document and are you challenging that they say that 10.000 of their troops were on the move?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see at the end of several lines there's a question, but this has continued on and on when there's a long, long statement with a small question on the end. And I just ask that Mr. Karadzic asks his questions simply to the witness and not make such statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By making such statements you are making the probative value of the witness very low. So put your questions in a simpler way. Put your questions one at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, please do not say how things should be; rather, give us an answer. Are you disputing that 10.000 soldiers left, as stated by this document of the Muslim secret service?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not disputing that 10.000 people left and they could have been having guns. But as for an organised division -- for a division to have broken through this way, it's completely incomprehensible. I don't believe it. But obviously in any war there has got to be propaganda. You have got to show that your people are many. That is common in any war. You have got to show that you are better equipped, you are heavier, you are more than your adversary. That is normal in any war. And you have got to give morale to your soldiers that still they are there. But for obvious reasons you really cannot have a division breaking through with, you know, 10.000 of them --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, Mr. Kingori, I have to intervene. What you are saying are logical inferences and I'm asking you about facts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the next paragraph which says that some army officers and the authorities evacuated their families abroad [In English] SVB -- [Interpretation] That's the one that begins with SVB of the 1st Corps and so on. Could we see the text a little bit further below so you can see the preparations for the liquidation of Serb civilians in case Zepa falls. Look below. [In English] "SVB of the 1st Corps is privy to information that after the fall of Srebrenica and the attack by the Chetniks on Zepa, a group has allegedly been formed consisting of the citizens of Zepa whose task is to select those Serbs who would be liquidated in case Zepa falls." [Interpretation] If we are talking logics, is it logical, Mr. Kingori, that all of this is going on without the military observers knowing?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is intelligence report gotten from your people and for in the military and especially an established military like the BSA, they had to get such intelligence and use it, maybe not necessarily directly, but indirectly. Maybe their plan was to eliminate those who are to eliminate the BSA senior guy -- the Serb senior guys who are in Zepa. So intelligence can be gotten through many ways, you had your own ways of getting this intelligence and utilising it. And the intelligence did not have to come to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your answer has one crucial deficiency. This is not an Army of Republika Srpska document. This is a document of the BH army. It's a Muslim document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the first page in the original. Although every page of the original bears the stamp of the Bosnian army. Can this document be admitted? I would like to see the original. You see this says Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It reports who arrived in Tuzla to Muslim territory. In e-court you see the Serbian version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's in the e-court. You have to switch to the e-court from ELMO. It's already there. We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1998, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, what did your service of military observers, Sector BH North-East, report to Zagreb about this event, the breakout of the Bosnian army, the losses of the Bosnian army during the breakout, the number of people who made it through, do you know what was reported? This was your direct command in Tuzla; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we reported on a possible route out for the Muslims, which was actually towards Tuzla, that we knew that would be the most possible route out. And we also talked about the fact that they had to fight their way out, we reported on that. They had to fight their way out because obviously they would not be given a safe route out to Tuzla. So that is what we reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That civilians would get a corridor or the 28th Division? Were we obligated to make it possible for the 28th Division to leave our territory peacefully, carrying weapons, and then from there attack us?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was very clear from the onset that you are not giving anybody a safe route out from the enclave because the BSA had already started the heavy bombardment of Srebrenica. And it was very clear from the onslaught -- onset that the aim was to clear the area of the Muslims, as had been told to us by Colonel Vukovic. So everything was evident, it was going as part of your plan. You had to clear the whole enclave of Muslims, which you did successfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, the Trial Chamber will decide that. I would kindly ask you to stick to the facts. Did your service report to Zagreb about this event and what did they say, how many combatants and how many people made it out with what kind of losses? Do you know about the losses of the 28th Division between Srebrenica and Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D4 -- 04768.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this a report from your north-east command in Zagreb, the UNMO headquarters in Zagreb, 17 July 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are these names familiar to you, who prepared this document and sent it to Major Kouznetsov and Mr. Woodhouse. Do you know these names?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know Woodhouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please scroll it down and when Mr. Kingori finishes reading, we can move to the next page. At the bottom it says: "Team Srebrenica are holding meetings tonight with representatives of the Serb side." Can we see the next page? Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I don't think we had the interpretation of your last comment, but we all can see this passage. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On 17 July did you have this meeting, were you there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had a meeting. I can't remember whether I was there or not, but we had a meeting, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see in the next paragraph that there are covered mortars mounted on Muslim trucks and did you know that Muslim troops were using mobile mortars to fire and then get away, hit and run in other words?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know what you are referring to because if it is the report in front of me, starting para 4, BiH side, this is not from Team Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But did you know about the phenomenon itself, that mortars would be placed on trucks, covered, they would fire from them, and then hide? Did you know that that's the way they used to deceive the UN?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I know is that when you are cornered you can do anything, so it's possible to have done that. But obviously you cannot cheat for a very long time without being discovered. But this is a report from Team Srebrenik, not Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Item D below. We don't have time for the rest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I would like the witness to read the item -- yes, D, capital D, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And there's a further passage on the next page, page 4.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, what is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The claims you made in your statement, aren't they inconsistent with what your command, the command of military observers, is reporting? Did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe I would like to know which claims, specific claims, you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The UN is confirming that a large number of combatants made it out of the area. Many got killed during the breakout, that Serb villages were burned on the way. They emerged into the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps. Correct? This whole item D, is it reflected in your statement? Does it make any impact on your statement? Is your statement consistent with this report of the military observers?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may we just go back to the first page because I think that might be what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This seems to be a report from the UNMO Sector North-East.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These headquarters, these staff headquarters, was it your command? Were you answerable to them, north-east?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So with all due respect, Mr. Kingori, I would say that your statement does not reflect and is not consistent with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, just a -- oh, yes, is that your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is: Why is your amalgamated statement so dramatically different from the official reports of your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't see any deviations from what has been reported here in that the crossing of these people, you can see in the report, is written they are armed with small arms, yeah, small arms. That does not -- and I still insist does not signify the arming of a division, anything above a section. So in essence what we are seeing, these are people who are armed. They could have been soldiers. They could have been just normal civilians who were armed. And as I said earlier, it goes beyond normal carrying of a gun to become a soldier. So it does not necessarily mean that all these were military people crossing over to the other side. However, the element of them burning the villages, because that is the other issue that you raised about when they were crossing, they have given the reasons why they were burning those villages, to get a wider area through which to cross and that is different from the burning of the village you talked about earlier. So it is not an inconsistency on my side at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're talking about squads and little groups again. Do you know that in the system of the former Yugoslavia each of these men had done his military service, gone through training, and were then part of the reserve force? All these men had regularly been called up to military drills at regular intervals. That was the system. It was a popular army, not a professional army. Did you take that into account?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, for sure, all this information we had. We had all this information, but we also know that some of them became soldiers by default. Some of them became armed by default. Not because they were trained but just because they happened to be of a good fighting age, just because they happened to be strong young men, they could just take a gun. That does not make one a soldier at all, just having a gun. Otherwise everybody, even those who were normally armed and they're not soldiers, would turn to soldiers. So in essence, what I'm trying to let the Court know is that 10.000 men in a division or a brigade or whatever you may call it does not go together hand in hand. You cannot have 10.000 men and say this is a division. It is not just the men. It is the men together with the equipment. And just small arms does not make someone a -- form a brigade just because you have small arms, it does not at all in any army whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you do not dispute that there were five brigades, 280th, 281st, 282nd, 283rd, 284th, and 285th, as well as several independent battalions, regardless of how well-equipped they were? You do not dispute that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move from the issue of the strength of that division or brigade. I think witness has answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, I'm looking through your paragraphs, paragraph 42 says there was no electricity. Did you know the Muslim side had sabotaged the transmission lines and, from that time onwards, neither Serbs nor Muslims had any electrical power?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did not know what had happened to the electricity. We just knew that it was not operating and we assumed it was damaged during the initial phases of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know how the protected areas were first established? On my orders the Serbian army stopped in 1993 at the entrance to Srebrenica. We accepted that Srebrenica become a protected area and there was no need whatsoever for a military organisation and armaments to exist there. We accepted all this and signed the agreement. When the weapons were taken away for safe keeping, there was no further need for those weapons to be there because the Serb side had accepted to have that area as a protected area.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm aware of all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, we'll discuss that after the break. Did you know that the Serb side in almost all peace agreements accepted that Zepa, Srebrenica, and many other areas in the Drina River Valley become constituent parts of the Muslim entity?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I knew is that Zepa was also a Muslim area, Srebrenica was a Muslim area, so the eventual situation did not come to our attention, whether it was to bring them together or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you can see the transcript, Mr. Kingori. Just the previous answer, did you say you were aware of it or you were not aware of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, they had written well and changed. I had said I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I note the time, Mr. Karadzic. We'll take a break for an hour and resume at 1.30. And we will admit that UNMO Zagreb report as Exhibit D1999.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Next is 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.31 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, I have to dispute, and I need to dispute, something in each of the paragraphs in the statement, sometimes entire paragraphs. I don't know if I will have time to do that. I will have to skip things now. Is it correct that you described your departure on the 13th of July to Srebrenica itself to the hospital in order to evacuate the sick?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't get what you mean by if I described my departure, but all I know is that I went back to Srebrenica to pick those who were left in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you look at your paragraph 183, for example, where you say that you think that you left Potocari on the 13th of July, and then you say that with a lady from the Medecins Sans Frontieres you went and you say that you saw a crater there and you did not have time to analyse it, this crater. However, at the beginning of the statement you speak about how you did actually conduct a crater analysis. Is that correct? You deal with this in paragraph 16. And you say that you were able to place equipment in the crater and to gauge the calibre and other things. Are you able to tell us what kind of equipment this is?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are several questions. I don't know how best to approach them because there's one on 183, there's another one on paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's stay with paragraph 16. Did you carry out crater analyses using equipment and can you tell us what sort of equipment it is that you used?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the crater analysis that we used to do -- we had some equipment that we could put on the hole that had been created, that is, the crater itself. For one, when a shell lands on a certain place, and especially if it is a hard point like on Tarmac or concrete, it forms a definite pattern, which can show you from which side the shell came from. You can see the way it has gone in and know this shell actually came from this direction because of the pattern that it forms. Secondly, we had some meters that we were using to put over the crater and also measure the depth, that is, the depth going in and also the width of the crater. With that we would be able to know the kind of weapon. It would guide us into knowing the kind of weapon, but it would be added -- we would have an added advantage of looking at the shrapnels, the fragments, of the crater -- of the shell which can help us identify the kind of weapon that has been used. After getting all these details, we would go to a book that we held and it would guide us into knowing the kind of weapon, the calibre, so that we could know the range. Because in the book it was indicated this calibre of weapon, this type of weapon, has got a range of this number of kilometres, 3 kilometres, 4 kilometres, or whatever, and then from there we could go to the map and put -- and get the estimate distance from the point of impact to where we thought that -- the launch of that weaponry could have taken place. We would get the grid reference of that particular point or grid square because definitely we used to give a bigger area because you cannot be very sure of the actual point where the weapon originated from. So that is how we used to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question just had to do with the equipment since it wasn't clear to me what sort of equipment this was. Is it a meter or did you have some other kind of equipment? What did you place into the crater?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had meters and calipers and we had -- there's another equipment that I cannot remember very well that -- I can't remember the name that would give us the general direction but those are the equipments we used to use. But I can hasten to add that when you get this, it just gives you an estimate of where the hardware could have come from. It gives you a general area, this is where it could have come from, and then you give that and for confirmation you can use normal patrols or inform the UN and they had their own ways of locating the actual place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you recall the equipment that you were not able to recall by the end of your testimony, could you please tell us the name of it so that we can find the characteristics of that equipment. What kinds of shells are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are talking about mortar shells, artillery shells, rockets, and also tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many analyses of mortar shells did you actually carry out?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did many.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what did you conclude and in what way? How did you determine the calibre, the direction, and the distance?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've just described that, but if you want me to go through it again I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We're just now talking about mortar shells; is that right? Would you go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the mortar shells it is the same thing. It used to have the same thing. You could easily be able to locate where it has coming from. It is the same thing. We used the same procedure, but of course there is the element of error which you can get in any way because maybe they have given a bigger charge or a lower charge depending on how far they want the shell to go. But of course that difference would not have been much. You would be able to get a grid -- a proper grid square of where the equipment is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how did you determine the calibre?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had an EOD, explosive ordnance depot, personnel from DutchBat who could help us do that. It was very easy because we just needed to carry the fragments, give it to them, or at times they could accompany us, and they could easily be able to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm surprised, Mr. Kingori, that you did not use the simplest means and that would be the examination of the tail fin. That would affect everything, would it not?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we used all that, even the tail fin, if it is there, if it is not fragmented. We used everything available, but as for the calibre, I've just told you the way we used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that sometimes the tail fin also gets fragmented so that you are not able to establish on the basis of the whole thing but on the basis of fragments what the calibre of the mortar shell is?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, at times even the tail fin was not easy to locate, was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How can we get any of your findings from those investigations? Is there a way to get that from you? Did you submit those findings in writing?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we used to submit them in writing to UNMO headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to ask the OTP to provide that for us because you are their witness. So you did have training in crater analysis for a few days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you were able to determine the calibre, the direction, and the distance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I've just said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Experts here have told us, however, that it was not possible to establish the distance in any event, especially when we're talking about mortar shells, possibly the direction and the longest range but not the distance and the co-ordinates. So could you please tell us how you managed to do that. Perhaps you should reveal that for them to know as well, and if you can, would you be able to do that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've already indicated how we used to do it. I've even talked about how we could be able to determine the range, we just go to the book and see the ranges of that particular kind of weapon. If it is between 2 and 3 kilometres, or maybe 5 kilometres, or whatever, we just go to the map, because we already know where we are and we already know the general direction, locate that on the map, the 4 or whatever kilometres, locate it on the map and get a grid square and that is what we used to give as the possible location of the equipment that fired that weapon. And I also added that when we give that to the UN, they had their own way on getting further information on the same because they had use of everything like satellites. But at least we have given them a general idea of where the weaponry is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A shell can come in from a range of 1 to 7 kilometres. How did you establish the range from which this -- the range of this incoming shell?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've just said the range is in the book that we were using. The ranges of different weaponry which were used in former Yugoslavia were already in a given book that we were using.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, there is a scale to the range from 1 to 7 kilometres. How did you determine the distance from which the shell came and establish the co-ordinates, also the grid for a particular weapon? How did you establish that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't get what you mean, the scale to the range from 1 to 7 kilometres. We were using the longest ranges which are given in the book, and you cannot have a range of between 1 and 7. You obviously know if it can hit 7 kilometres it can also hit even 1 kilometre, but it would be not effective. That is for one. Secondly, it would be of no use to the people who were firing it, so we were using the longer ranges, and I don't think there is a range that is normally given of 1 to 7. The effective ranges are the ones which are given and that is what we use. Like even small arms, small arms like a rifle, you would be told is between 5- and 600 metres. It does not mean it cannot fire 50 metres, it can. But we're talking about the ranges, the longer ranges, that will be effective.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is the shortest distance from which you could fire an 82-millimetre mortar shell and what is the longest distance? If you establish the direction, all right, very well, but what is the closest and the farthest reach of that particular mortar so that it would be able to hit that particular crater? It can be from 1500 metres or from 7.000 metres; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, you don't expect me to remember all the technical details. For this one I cannot remember obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But any mortar operator would know that, that you can fire at close range and at a long range. How did you determine the grid and how did you decide, out of that range of several kilometres that are possible, how did you zone in to a particular location or a distance?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've already gone through this. I've explained how we used to get it. I've also explained how we used to get the grid square or the grid reference of the particular area that we thought the weapon would be firing from. And I really don't see why you want me to repeat the same again because I am not saying anything that I should add on the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were these Serbian shells that were dropping on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was the calibre of those shells that were dropping on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there were various and we put them in our reports. Some of them would be 105, 155, and even mortars, 60-millimetre mortars, and all those kind of weaponry. We could analyse and get them and report on the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do we agree that there are 60-millimetre, 82-millimetre, and 120-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there were so many types, so many types, and it's all in that book. Whatever was used to fire is what we used to analyse and this is what we wrote on, not necessarily all the weaponry in the BSA arsenal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But two armies, the two armies that you were observing, the Army of Republika Srpska and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, had identical weapons. Did they have any other mortars other than those of these three calibres, 60, 82, and 120 millimetres?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what we were analysing was incoming, incoming weapons, not outgoing. If there was any outgoing, that is the one that could have come from the BiH, it could have been analysed by other people, not us, because we were analysing what was coming into the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Incoming shells. What is the longest reach or range of 60-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have those details with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was the distance? How far was the line of separation from the centre of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, that is a very difficult question in that -- unless you are specific because Srebrenica from Yellow Bridge is a certain number of kilometres. Srebrenica from former OP Echo is different from any other section of the enclave. So the cease-fire line really had different distances from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the closest and what was its furthest point from measuring from the centre of Srebrenica to the first Serb positions in all directions, did you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had not kept those measurements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that an incoming 60-millimetre mortar shell would call for you to determine whether this had come in from Serb positions or whether it was coming from Muslim territory?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are two issues here. A 60-millimetre mortar launched from the direction of OP Echo or thereabouts or anywhere at the cease-fire line towards Srebrenica will hit Srebrenica, not necessarily in the town but the enclave. It would hit the enclave, and you still go there and analyse and get to know that it is a 60-millimetre mortar from a certain distance outside the cease-fire line. But at the same time, we were not aware that the Muslims could fire at themselves, so we could not imagine the Muslim side firing at their Muslim brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know how many killings there were in Srebrenica itself and did you know that Srebrenica was led by a bandit leadership that foreign observers and DutchBat soldiers described as a gang and criminals, rapes, killings, prostitution, smuggling, all possible kinds of criminal acts, did you know that?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'll skip that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Mr. Kingori, that your seven-day training was not enough. Would you agree? We've heard experts here who have dealt with this their entire lives, crater analysis I mean, and nobody told us what you are telling us now.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, my seven-days' training was not a basic training. It was training to senior officers, not just myself alone, to senior officers who were -- who had experience in the military. So it's just confirmation and reconfirmation of some issues. It's not basic training. And I also said whatever we were getting were estimates and that is what we would give, and that could give a proper assessment of the area from where the firing would have come from and that proved very useful to the UN because they didn't have to concentrate on the whole location where the BSA were. We guided them into particular areas. Like the rocket-launcher that was coming beyond Yellow Bridge, it was shelling from, you know, beyond Yellow Bridge, we knew where it was and we say the same. And even when we went to Potocari -- actually after the fall of the enclave, the rocket-launcher actually came from the same direction. So we could have been slightly not very accurate in terms of maybe millimetres, metres, or whatever, but at least we give a general direction which is what was required from our mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thus, at the critical time in July, the two of you, because the third one was already in hospital, informed the Dutch Battalion about the fire from the Serb side; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were aware of what was happening. We knew where this fire could have come from, and we were correct as far as we knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it possible that you had too much trust in your Muslim guides and interpreters who misinformed you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would be incorrect because we also had our own -- we were -- we were intelligent also in a way, in that we were hearing the shell -- the shells overflying or coming from whatever direction and hitting certain areas, and the only time that we relied on the interpreter was when we sent him to Srebrenica because it was no longer safe for us to be there. That is the time we sent him and he was able to give us where the shells were actually hitting. That does not mean ourselves were not hearing them overflying where we were or even hear them land. It's only that we could not get the actual location at which we were guided into the actual location by the interpreter, so he could not cheat us -- I mean, he could not lie to us on something that we have also heard ourselves.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we briefly look at P4152.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, do you know that both the Doctors Without Borders and UNPROFOR reported that Serbs were not hitting buildings or features but they were firing around to prevent movement, so-called barrage fire, to prevent movement? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I know is what we reported on. That is what I knew. And the shelling was actually not aimed at certain areas and leaving out others. Nobody can tell that that shelling was not directed at buildings. The fact that it did not hit buildings does not mean it was not directed at buildings. It could have just missed by good luck. And as it was in our report, we were even surprised that the number of casualties were so low, and especially knowing that even our building, the PTT, was targeted and missed several times, that even the hospital was targeted and missed several times. So when somebody says houses were not aimed at, really I cannot understand. I cannot understand. I cannot comprehend that. What I can say is they were missed, some of them were missed, and that was just by good luck and I'm happy that they were missed, otherwise the destruction, the suffering, the death could have been astronomical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What would be your basis of conclusion that PTT building as well as hospitals were targeted but missed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, when these artillery or weapons are aimed at a certain place, there are different variations in that you aim to get a certain point but you may miss that point because of where you are launching the weapon from. Artillery weapons are normally launched from behind a hill, where they are safer and they cannot be seen directly by the enemy, and that is why they are called high trajectory. They go up very high and then land somewhere. So -- and if that -- that weapon is aimed at a certain building, you would definitely know in that it would miss, either go on top, fly overhead, go to the side, one side or the other side, and you would see some corrections because they normally make corrections when you aim and do not get your target, because I believe they had their own people on ground. You change the -- either the charge or direction, you move it towards -- you correct the direction a bit, and that is the time you would see if it was hitting to the left, you see now it's hitting maybe slightly more to the right. If it was hitting far much overhead, you see now it is hitting slightly lower. So it was very easy to know a targeted place, very easy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that tank produces indirect fire?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you did say, look here, that the tank 84 -- do you know at the time it was the most powerful, the best tank that could hit and fire unmistakably even when the tank was crossing dunes and going across holes. You say here the Serb 84 tank was in position. Are you trying to say that it missed by chance?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I kindly request you show me where I said a tank produces indirect fire. I never mentioned that. I've never mentioned it in my report, and what I have in my report is a tank produces direct fire. And that is why when we saw tanks located some distance, about 2 kilometres from our PTT building, we decided to leave because it produces direct fire. So what you are saying, I'm not aware, I've not said anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, here, on the 10th of July, you record the presence of a tank, state-of-the-art tank at the time in the world, with state-of-the-art firing devices, and you say that the Serbs were missing their targets in a non-deliberate way. You are ascribing bad intentions to Serbs, whereas you saw with your own eyes the T-84 tank that could hit precisely any window that was targeted.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have a paragraph number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, did the witness say in his statement that the tank actually targeted the building? I'm reading paragraph 102 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm now talking about the document before us in e-court, it's a document from this service, their own observer mission. It notes the presence of a tank on the 10th of July. In the meantime, Mr. Kingori is saying that the Serbs were using heavy artillery, shooting to hit, but they were missing because they were shooting from beyond a hill by indirect fire. However, the Serbs had a tank and they could see it. The tank was able to use direct fire unmistakably, and I am disputing Mr. Kingori's allegation. I put it to him that he was biassed against the Serbs in ascribing them ill intentions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you are not making statements here. You ask questions. Put your questions one at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here is the question: You claim the Serbs were missing because they were shooting with indirect fire from behind a hill. If they really wanted to hit the target, why didn't they use the T-84 tank that could hit with precision any window?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we are mixing two issues, that of the tank and that of the high-trajectory artillery weapons, in that when I mentioned about the high-trajectory artillery weapons, that's when I said they were missing the target. But later on is when I brought in or we brought in the issue of the tank, which could easily be seen from a certain location, which I have indicated. So these are two different things in two different areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's clear one thing up. Look at this document. From whom did you receive this information? Are all of these your direct observations or did you receive some reports from someone?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report came from us, and if we have not said not confirmed by us, it is us who had confirmed. So it is true it was like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you now if the Serbs' intention was to hit and they were missing because fire was indirect, from behind a hill, why did they continue, on the 10th of July, to fire from behind a hill when they could have used the T-84 tank which certainly wouldn't have missed?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the tacticians are the ones who should be asked that, the people from the BSA side. But all I know is that they had almost finished their job. By the 10th, they were almost through with their job so they did what they were doing. They had already softened Srebrenica. They had already done enough damage. People had already started getting scared. So everything was almost through. So in fact, the use of the tank could not have been very essential because, after all, if they were coming to reclaim the enclave, as they had said, that is, the BSA, obviously they would not have wanted to destroy most of the buildings that they were planning to come and use. So maybe they -- these were obvious tactical or tactical reasons of not damaging everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, intentions are debatable. I kindly ask you to tell me first who informed you about these events in Srebrenica which you were not there to see for yourself? In paragraph -- first of all, who informed you [In English] "the heavy shells probably" and so on -- [Interpretation] About this, the second part of the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this information could have come from our yellow card, that is, the interpreter; but at the same time we had the MSF person who was in contact with some other people in the hospital and you could be able to get some information from there. The point at hand is of the shelling of the hospital which we could really get that it was being targeted and missed by a few metres and there was no dispute to that because even when I went back there later I confirmed that, that it has been -- actually, it had been hit around the hospital and also in the Bravo Company of DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Kingori, how could you possibly know that the hospital -- how far is it -- you were in Potocari. How far are Potocari from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was far. It was not that near, but we could be able to get from the sources that I've already told you about. It was far, but the shells we could hear. It is only that the actually landing area of the shell we could not be able to get. But I've given you the source of the -- that information on where the shells were landing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at paragraph 121 of your statement, did your interpreter have one week's training or not even that? You were only two. The hospital in Srebrenica is far from you. You get your information from a Muslim who is partial. It is in his interest to blame the Serbs. He has only one week's training and you accept him at his word. You take his word for it that the Serbs were targeting the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the issue of the interpreter being trained for one week does not arise. That interpreter had a lot of experience. We found them there and they had worked there for over two years. So they are people who were very experienced in identifying what was an incoming shell and also where it was hitting. It was very easy for them to know. They had very good experience of their work as interpreters. And also having worked with UNMOs gave them an upper hand in knowing some of the things which were happening in a war zone, like it was at that time. I also said that immediately after that I left for Srebrenica and I noticed that everything that we had been told had actually happened and it's in my report. I found that the hospital had actually been targeted. I also found that the areas around had been damaged. The road had been cratered. The DutchBat Company -- the outside of the DutchBat Company had also been cratered, you know, through heavy artillery weapons. So all that we came to believe is actually what had happened and we had not exaggerated anything at all. As for him being a Muslim, I don't think we had issues to do with his background at that particular moment. What we had was knowing what was happening at that particular moment and reporting on the same. Of course, as I said earlier, the UN had its own other systems of verifying this information. And that is why they were even able to get the targets which we had not been -- we had not given and used air power to actually attack those targets. So I think that is the answer I can give to the questions you have asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, those other sources of information in the area of Sarajevo established more than once that military observers were useless and pointless. This incident happened at 11.26 and you are writing your report based on information received from a man who is biased, who belongs to one of the warring parties --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- and still you put his words in your report --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first sentence of this question is not a question at all and has nothing to do with it, it's a statement. And then he started -- I thought it was going to end in a question but didn't. This has gone on several times today and I would ask the accused to just ask simple questions and we can get through this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I totally agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, on my assessment, you're using between one-third and half of your time today in making statements and it sits ill with the complaint that you don't have enough time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I am challenging this way of thinking and making conclusions, which is groundless, in order to help Mr. Kingori to realise his mistake and I want him to answer what I'm asking, not what I'm not asking. But I'll narrow it down even further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When was this report sent? Isn't the time indicated as 11.26?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, where is the time you are reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Line 1, at the top of the document. While we're waiting for the document, when did the incident occur?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We don't need the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know why we lost the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see it says the incident happened at 11.00 and you are reporting at 11.26, based on information you received from the interpreter; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think you are putting the words in my mouth. I didn't just say the interpreter. I mentioned other sources. And 11.26 is the time of transmission, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Look at paragraph 121 of your statement now. You say that you were informed that 155-millimetre artillery shells were hitting the direct surrounding of the hospital. And in my previous question I also referred to the environs of the hospital. For the record, you said "yellow card." That means Emir; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you go to Srebrenica on the 10th or on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what you said before, that you first verified and then wrote your report, is not true. You could not have done that by 11.26 on the 10th. You were in Srebrenica only on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said I verified that report that it was correct when I went back to Srebrenica, and obviously that was not on the 10th. I said I went on the 13th. But could I have gone back there and found something different, I could have just written again and say I found a different thing all together and that whatever we had sent earlier was wrong. Then, if you allow me, I can go back to the issue where you talked about military observers being useless. That is actually something that is not right to say because I don't believe the whole UN system would be that -- will just, you know, appoint observers if they don't know what they are doing. They would not appoint somewhere to go somewhere, do something, and they know they are useless. I don't think they can form such a system. Just because they don't fit what you would like them to fit or do the way you would like them to do doesn't make them useless at all. And that is why, due to the essence of these observers, they are everywhere in every mission that you ever see. Wherever there is a military issue, there must be military observers, contributed by the countries which have contributed troops to that particular theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I did not say that you were useless, sir. It was the highest commanders of the UNPROFOR who said that military observers were useless. It was just an answer to your claims that you never made any mistakes. Look at paragraph 183. Who were you in the hospital with? It's actually paragraphs 185 and 186, where you describe the treatment three Serb soldiers gave to three ill women. Who were you with there? Were you alone?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was with an MSF lady, I think her name was Christine or Christina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Anybody else?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there were other people. We found some injured, some people who were admitted. We've -- the list is there, we have indicated, the sick, even the number of the sick that we found there, I have indicated there, and there was some BSA soldiers around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at paragraph 184 and particularly 185, and also 106, how you smear Serbian soldiers. You say that they threatened old women and you use a euphemism when you say "a bit hostile," "that was a bit hostile." I wouldn't say that. I would say it was drastic, drastically hostile. Actually, did that happen at all?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, because I'm the one who was there, I said what I saw, I said what I heard. So maybe you were in a different position all together. You may -- I know you were not in that particular area so I don't think it would be right for you to change what I saw or what I heard because I didn't report from anybody else. I was there personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D4970, can we have that without having it broadcast, though. I think that it is under an embargo.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a -- thank you, Your Honour. This is the document that I spoke of earlier, and even if we don't broadcast it, I can't imagine we're going to have a discussion that isn't going to reveal what type of a document it is. So I would ask that we stay in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The lady you mentioned is reporting and she's saying that she's going with Franken, somebody from the Army of Republika Srpska, and a UNMO to the hospital to see all the wounded. [In English] "I have to close the Telex now ..." and so on. [Interpretation] Can we have page 14 now. Could all the participants take a look at this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this in e-court or on Sanction?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] E-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could all please take a look at this so that I don't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And let me ask you, sir, you so vilify the Serbs that no one else who was in the same places as you were never wrote anything remotely similar or said anything remotely similar. That is why I'm challenging your entire statement. Why did this lady not describe these drastic threats issued to old women, people saying that they would be killed?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm the one who heard that, I'm the one who was told that, I wrote about it, and I still maintain that was correct as far as the statement was made. Secondly, the issue of me being against one side or the other should not be raised at all because I had no reason to favour one side or the other as a person or even as a Kenyan. We had no strategic importance of that area as a country, nothing that would have swayed me into saying something that is not true as far as I was concerned because there was no reason for that. Kenya does not have any -- did not have any strategic, you know, importance to any part of former Yugoslavia. So really, I was saying what I was told, what I heard. Maybe others could have heard other things, maybe they could have seen things differently or maybe they were not exactly in the same location that I was told these things. And furthermore, this was not even the first time we were being told about BSA killing the Muslims. Colonel Vukovic told us the same and we reported on the same, that they were going to clear the enclave. So it's not the first time that this is being heard from the BSA --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get to Vukovic, sir, we'll get to Vukovic, sir. This is what I'm interested in now. This lady, who is not sparing the Serbs in the least, she is saying they are robbing people, taking property --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the witness has answered the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could these two pages be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What pages are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 13 and 14 in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under seal, that will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2000, under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move into open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 186 you say that you physically helped her go. You lifted her yourself. Did anyone else describe that in their daily reports?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what others were writing in their daily reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you report?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we see your report of the 13th of July where you say that Serbs mistreat old women who are sick, forcing them to evacuate from the hospital? Show us this report of yours.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you can look for the reports, situation reports, and get them, well and good. But I don't think you have all the situation reports. All I know is that we reported on the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now we are going to go back to what it was that you discussed with Major Nikolic and Colonel Vukovic. You said that there was socialising involved as well and coffee and brandy. However, you say that what they said to you was heard at official meetings where minutes were being kept; right? You say that they said that they wanted all of Srebrenica for themselves and that all the Muslims should be evacuated or moved out; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I said is that in one of the meetings that we had held with Colonel Vukovic - and actually it's not the first one - he told us that -- he asked us what the UN might do if the BSA attacked the enclave. And he's recorded. He's in documents, he asked that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But -- well, it's possible that he asked you that. But why did you then say that he had said to you that he would free the entire enclave of Muslims, that that was the Serb intention? Did you report about that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I did. I just mentioned, if you look at my answer there, I just mentioned about one. That is just one of them. There is another time that he said that they would clear the whole enclave of the Muslims, and clearing, obviously they meant they would kill everybody. He said that, he mentioned that, and I reported on the same. And also, if I may add, he said if they want to leave the enclave, he can provide a safe route out from the enclave. He offered that also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you include that in your daily report?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you show that to us?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
